tagline.text: The Trappist monastery in Jordan, known for mango jam and quiet retreats

location.label: Location
location.text: San Miguel, Jordan, Guimaras (Abbey of Our Lady of the Philippines)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (a retreat is 1 night or more)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (per person, transport from Jordan and souvenirs, lodging extra)

children.text: The Abbey of Our Lady of the Philippines is a Cistercian monastery founded in 1972 in San Miguel, Jordan, and is one of only two Trappist monasteries in the country. Admission is free, and it is a leading Guimaras stop for buying products made by the monks, such as mango jam and pineapple jam, and for a quiet rest.

The Abbey of Our Lady of the Philippines is in San Miguel, Jordan, on Guimaras Island. According to Wikipedia, it was founded on August 31, 1972 by Trappist monks of the US Region, became a priory on May 20, 1982 and was raised to an abbey on October 29, 1990. It is one of only two Trappist monasteries in the Philippines and belongs to the Cistercian (Trappist) Order in the Archdiocese of Jaro. It is in Jordan, the first place you reach when you cross from Iloilo by boat, so it is often chosen as the first stop of an overland tour of Guimaras. The current abbot is introduced as Dom Kevin Lipasan, and the official website is olpabbey.org. "Trappist" refers to Cistercian monks of the strict observance, and knowing that this is a community that lives by prayer and work makes a visit more meaningful.

What makes the place famous among visitors is the products the monks make themselves. Wikipedia says pineapple jam and mango jam are sold under the name Trappist Monastic Products and can be bought in local stores and at the monastery's shop. According to one visitor's account, the monastery also makes jellies, jams, candies, piyaya and sweet mango products, using ingredients grown on its own land. Next to the roadside souvenir shop is the newest addition, a coffee shop, where buses and cars can easily stop.

The monastery is the home of a religious community before it is a tourist facility. One blog describes it as a quiet, sacred place suited to self-reflection and group spiritual retreats. There is a guest house where visitors can stay, and one guide says a day's stay with meals starts from about

(check the current rate with the monastery). The author of that post stayed nearly a week and talked with four of the monks, all of whom were friendly and thoughtful. The chapel is said to be open daily, but specific hours could not be confirmed, so follow the guidance on site.

If you want one quiet place in a Guimaras trip that is not a beach or waterfall, this is the first place to think of. Around Jordan Wharf there is the "Smallest Plaza," once recognized by Guinness World Records as the smallest plaza in the world, which is free and said to be open 24 hours. The National Mango Research Center on the way to the monastery is also free to enter and sells mango seedlings. Combining the monastery, plaza and research center lets you take in a first impression of Guimaras economically in half a day.
The chapel is said to be open daily. One blog recommends visiting the chapel first on a first trip. Walk quietly and take photos only where allowed.

blocks.title: Monastery gift shop and coffee shop

children.text: The gift shop has moved to the roadside, where buses and cars can stop easily, and a coffee shop is right next to it. You can rest over local coffee and snacks.
Besides jam, there are said to be jellies, candies, piyaya (a Filipino flat pastry) and sweet mango foods. They make good snacks or gifts on a trip.
One guide says the guest house starts from about
a day with meals. It is beside the road and easy to find, and is said to suit a quieter, more private stay. Ask the monastery directly about reservations and rules.

A visitor who stayed several days at the guest house reports talking with four monks, all friendly and thoughtful. There are community living areas, so do not enter places without guidance, and speak politely when you approach someone.

The mango research center on the main road in San Miguel, Jordan, is free to enter and has a large mango plantation and research and packaging buildings. You can also buy mango seedlings, and opening hours are not given, so check locally.
Arrive at Jordan Wharf, stop by the tourism office and find a tricycle.
Go to the monastery (about 20–30 minutes by tricycle).
Look around the chapel and pray or rest quietly.
Browse jam and snacks at the gift shop and buy gifts.
Rest at the coffee shop and continue your itinerary.
Some sources suggest monastery visits are mostly in the morning, so an itinerary that stops there first in the morning is convenient.
Charter a tricycle for the day at Jordan Wharf.
See the Smallest Plaza and the National Mango Research Center.
Visit the Trappist Monastery and buy jam and snacks.
Have lunch (at a restaurant known for mango pizza, for example) and head to Guisi Lighthouse.
See Guisi Lighthouse and Guisi Beach.
Tour Alubihod Beach and return to Jordan.

A monastery visit is a short indoor and outdoor stop, so the weather does not matter much. But because there is overland travel on the island, the drier dry season is more comfortable.
In the third week of April the island holds a mango festival, so you can feel the atmosphere of mango season. Plan your monastery visit mostly for the morning.

To stay at the monastery, use the guest house. One guide says a day with meals starts from about

and recommends it for those who want a quieter, more private stay. Reservation methods and rules must be asked about directly, and one guide lists a contact number of (033) 581-3385, among others. Numbers can change, so check. Many ordinary tourists use lodging at Alubihod Beach or in the town of Jordan.

For meals, use the coffee shop next to the monastery and restaurants around Jordan. Tour courses often include lunch at a restaurant known for mango pizza. Guimaras is famous for mangoes, so in season try some.

Visit the monastery in the morning. One guide gives the hours as 8:30 AM–12:00 noon.
Move quietly and do not talk loudly on the phone. Modest clothing is recommended.
Jam is popular as a gift, so compare prices at the monastery shop and in local stores.
Take photos on the grounds only where allowed, and do not photograph the monks without permission.
If you want a retreat, first contact the monastery to confirm the rules and available dates.
Bring small bills. The shop may be short of change.
Asking the tourism office at Jordan Wharf about tricycle fares and itineraries is convenient.
According to one guide, adding the wind farm to a tricycle island loop costs about ₱300 more. If you only want the monastery, you do not need that stop.
The Smallest Plaza near Jordan Wharf is free, so look around while you wait for your boat.
The monastery is the living space of a community that prays and works. Visiting hours and the areas open to visitors may change, so follow the guidance and behave quietly.
Visiting hours (8:30 AM–noon) and gift shop hours (9 AM–5 PM) differ by source, so confirm on site.
Contact numbers and lodging rates come from sources dated 2019–2022. Check directly with the monastery before you visit.
During services, avoid noise and movement, and access may be restricted.
Boat and overland fares differ by source and may change, so check before you depart.
Do not damage plants or facilities on the grounds or leave trash behind.
There is a lot of travel outdoors and the midday sun is strong. Bring a hat and water, and withdraw cash in Iloilo beforehand.
